# Beer distribution game

Build the classic beer distribution game. Four companies form a supply chain for one product: a retailer, a wholesaler, a distributor and a factory, each run by an AI agent. Every week, customers buy from the retailer; weekly customer demand is random, a whole number of cases between 0 and 8. Each week every company ships what it can to the company below it, then places an order with the company above it (the factory instead starts production). Orders reach the supplier the following week, and shipments take two weeks to arrive; production also takes two weeks. Everyone starts with 12 cases in stock and 4 cases already on the way on each shipping link. Demand a company cannot fill becomes backlog and must be shipped later. Each company pays $0.50 per case in stock and $1.00 per case of backlog at the end of every week. Companies only see their own stock, backlog, incoming orders and deliveries, never the others' positions. The game lasts 20 weeks and the team's goal is the lowest total cost.

## Deliverables

Report these outputs:
- `customer_demand` — a list of the cases customers demanded each week, in week order.
- `factory_orders` — a list of the cases the factory put into production each week, in week order.
- `costs_by_role` — a map from role ("retailer", "wholesaler", "distributor", "factory") to that company's total cost.
- `total_team_cost` — the sum of all four companies' costs.
- `bullwhip_ratio` — the variance of the factory's weekly production orders divided by the variance of weekly customer demand.


Build this environment. Save it with write_contract and use the other tools as you see fit. Reply without calling a tool when you are done.

BRIEF:
# Beer distribution game
You run one company in a four-stage beer supply chain: factory -> distributor -> wholesaler -> retailer -> customers. The game lasts 20 weeks. Everyone starts with 12 cases in stock, and 4 cases are already on the way to each company on its shipping link (arriving in week 1). Weekly customer demand for the retailer is a random whole number of cases from 0 to 8. Each week every company ships what it can to the company below it, then decides how much to order from the company above it (the factory instead starts production).

## Rules
Each week, in order: (1) cases shipped two weeks ago arrive and are added to your stock; (2) orders placed on you last week become due; (3) you ship as much as you can -- min(stock, backlog + orders due) -- to your customer, and whatever you cannot ship becomes backlog; (4) you place exactly one order with your supplier, which reaches them next week (the factory sends its order into production). Shipments and production take two weeks to arrive: cases you ship this week are added to your customer's stock two weeks later. At the end of every week you pay $0.50 per case held in stock and $1.00 per case of backlog. Unfilled customer demand is backlog too and must be shipped later. You see only your own stock, backlog, orders received, arrivals, shipments, orders you placed and cost -- never another company's position. The team's goal is the lowest total cost across all four companies.

## You
You are Retailer (company, id retailer).
You are the Retailer. Place one order per week with your supplier.
Act only through your tools. Your turn ends when you take a final action or call end_turn.

The environment is complete, checked, and verified. Here's what I built and why it's faithful.

## `scenario.json` — Beer distribution game

**Structure**
- **Four agent companies** (`retailer → wholesaler → distributor → factory`), each with private `stock`, `backlog`, incoming-order/delivery records, an order history, and a running `cost`.
- **Clock**: 20 weeks (bound to `$inputs.weeks`), one order per week per company.
- **World pipelines**: `orders_next` (orders placed this week, due to each supplier next week), and a two-stage transit buffer `transit_1`/`transit_2` keyed by receiver — so every shipment and production batch takes exactly two weeks to arrive.

**Round mechanics** (start event, runs before any agent acts, so it is order-independent):
1. Arrivals from `transit_1` enter stock; `transit_1 := transit_2`; `transit_2 := 0`.
2. Orders placed last week become due (`incoming_order`); customer demand `$randint(0, $inputs.demand_max)` is drawn and assigned to the retailer.
3. Shipping: `ship = min(stock, backlog + incoming_order)`; unmet demand becomes backlog; the shipped cases are routed into the customer's two-week transit.
4. Agents then each place exactly one order (`must_act`); the factory's order routes into `transit_2[factory]` as production.
- **End event** charges `$0.50 × stock + $1.00 × backlog` per company per week.

**Outputs** delivered exactly as specified: `customer_demand`, `factory_orders`, `costs_by_role`, `total_team_cost`, and `bullwhip_ratio` (population variance of factory orders ÷ variance of demand, guarded against empty/zero cases).

**Verification performed**
- `fg_env.check` → no issues, including a played round.
- Hand-derived the idle-retailer cost from seed 7's demand: 17 backordered cases cost $697 + $10.50 holding = **$707.50** at 20 weeks; the engine returned exactly that. Re-derived the week-1 isolated figure ($639.50) and matched it too — confirming arrival timing, backlog accounting, and cost formulas.
- Confirmed a bug I fixed during authoring: the initial-pipeline event had inverted its role test, giving stock to the factory instead of the retailer; preview exposed it, and I corrected it to `up_idx >= 0` (anyone with a supplier gets an incoming pipeline). Factory now correctly starts at 12 cases.
- Idle and random runs both complete cleanly; `bullwhip_ratio` returns `null` (not an error) when no orders are placed.

**Assumptions / inputs**: `start_stock` (12), `pipeline` (4 per link), `holding_cost` ($0.50), `backlog_cost` ($1.00), `demand_max` (8), `order_cap` (200), `weeks` (20) are all configurable knobs, so the rules genuinely change with the inputs. Agents see only their own position, pipeline, and order history; an omniscient spectator view is provided for reports only.

qty.description: Cases to order (factory: cases to produce).

order.outcome: You placed an order for {$params.qty} cases; it reaches your supplier next week (the factory's order goes into production and arrives in two weeks).

stages.name: decisions
stages.brief: Decide how much to order from your supplier this week (the factory decides how much to produce).

position.title: Your position
position.show: Stock {stock} cases | backlog {backlog} cases | orders due this week (received) {received} | cases delivered to you this week {delivered} | cases you shipped this week {shipped}

pipeline.title: Incoming pipeline
pipeline.show: Arriving next week: {$get($world.transit_1, $actor.idx, 0)} cases | arriving in two weeks: {$get($world.transit_2, $actor.idx, 0)} cases

all_positions.title: Supply chain (omniscient)
all_positions.show: {name}: stock {stock}, backlog {backlog}, received {received}, shipped {shipped}, order {last_order}, cost {$it.cost|money}

customer_demand.description: Cases customers demanded each week, in week order

factory_orders.description: Cases the factory put into production each week, in week order

total_team_cost.description: Sum of the four companies' costs

bullwhip_ratio.description: Variance of weekly factory production orders divided by variance of weekly customer demand

invariants.why: Stock and backlog can never be negative.
A company places at most one order per week.
